claims.claim: Hardware AES (x86 AES-NI + PCLMULQDQ for GHASH, VAES/AVX-512 on newer CPUs,

makes AES-GCM several times faster **and** constant
time.
Software AES with lookup tables is slow and leaks via cache timing.
claims.evidence_quote: its performance on platforms that lack such hardware is considerably lower. yet another problem is that many aes implementations are vulnerable to cache- collision timing attacks

claims.claim: grep -o -w -E 'aes|pclmulqdq|vaes|vpclmulqdq|avx512f' /proc/cpuinfo | sort | uniq -c
grep -o -w -E 'aes|pmull|sha2' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u
sysctl -a | grep -i 'hw.optional.arm.FEAT_AES'

Hypervisors sometimes mask CPU flags (old CPU models in VM configs, some
nested setups).

If `aes` is missing inside a VM on modern hardware, fix the VM
CPU model (`host-passthrough`) rather than accepting slow crypto.
openssl speed -evp aes-128-gcm -seconds 2
OPENSSL_ia32cap="~0x200000200000000" openssl speed -evp aes-128-gcm -seconds 2
The mask clears bit 57 (AES-NI)
claims.evidence_quote: bit #54 denoting availability of movbe instruction; bit #57 denoting aes-ni instruction set extension

claims.claim: bit 33 (PCLMULQDQ) of the capability vector
claims.evidence_quote: bit #33 denoting availability of pclmulqdq instruction; bit #41 denoting ssse3, supplemental sse3, support

claims.claim: A large drop (often 5-10x) confirms the accelerated path was in use.

If both
runs are equally slow, the build or CPU lacks acceleration.
`openssl version -a` shows `CPUINFO: OPENSSL_ia32cap=...` in 3.x builds
non-default environment variable value here means someone has masked features.
claims.evidence_quote: now the only way to affect the capability detection is to set openssl_ia32cap environment variable prior target application start

claims.claim:
AES hardware present (servers, modern laptops, ARMv8 phones): AES-128-GCM
  or AES-256-GCM.
claims.evidence_quote: while aes is very fast on dedicated hardware, its performance on platforms that lack such hardware is considerably lower

claims.claim:
No AES hardware (older/low-end ARM, many MCUs without AES peripheral):
  ChaCha20-Poly1305 - fast in software
claims.evidence_quote: it is considerably faster than aes in software-only implementations, making it around three times as fast on platforms that lack specialized aes hardware

claims.claim: and constant time without tables.
claims.evidence_quote: the operations used in chacha20 are all additions, xors, and fixed rolls. all of these can and should be implemented in constant time

claims.claim:
TLS stacks (BoringSSL, Go, OpenSSL with `SSL_OP_PRIORITIZE_CHACHA`) can
  prefer ChaCha20 when the client lists it first, signalling no AES hardware.

On MCUs, use the AES peripheral via the vendor HAL or mbedTLS alt
implementations;

check the peripheral handles key/IV loading without leaving
key material in readable registers after use.

coverage: I extracted every command and flag (the three /proc/cpuinfo/sysctl CPU-flag greps, both openssl speed -evp aes-128-gcm -seconds 2 invocations and the OPENSSL_ia32cap=~0x200000200000000 mask), every number and setting (bit 57, bit 33, the 5-10x figure, 3.x builds, AES-128-GCM/AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, SSL_OP_PRIORITIZE_CHACHA, host-passthrough, mbedTLS) and every behaviour claim (software-AES cache leakage, the AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ/VAES/ARMv8 enumeration, hypervisor flag masking, the openssl version -a CPUINFO note, the env-var masking meaning, the three AEAD-choice bullets and the MCU register guidance), treating the Verify checklist as procedural restatements of already-checked behaviours; the OPENSSL_ia32cap man page confirmed the bit 57/bit 33 mappings and the env-var masking mechanism, RFC 8439 confirmed the cache-timing, AES-hardware-performance and ChaCha20 software/constant-time claims, the Intel article (HTTP 403 to the attestation fetch, so omitted from sources) gates the AES-NI speedup and constant-time claims, and no listed source covers the /proc/cpuinfo, sysctl, QEMU host-passthrough, TLS-stack and MCU specifics.
suggested_edits: Replace the Intel article, which returns 403 Forbidden to automated fetchers, with a fetchable AES-NI performance source covering the 'several times faster', '5-10x' and constant-time claims; add sources for the unsupported specifics: Linux /proc/cpuinfo and macOS sysctl hw.optional.arm.FEAT_AES CPU flags, QEMU host-passthrough VM CPU model, the OpenSSL SSL_OP_PRIORITIZE_CHACHA option (ssl(7) man page), the openssl version -a CPUINFO line, and ARMv8/mbedTLS MCU documentation; the bit 57/bit 33 mask mapping and the OPENSSL_ia32cap env-var semantics are confirmed by the listed man page and the cache-timing/ChaCha20 claims by RFC 8439.
